newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy cuts discount rate after inflation fall.
newsitem.headline: Italy cuts discount rate after inflation fall.

text.p: The Bank of Italy, acting after a steady decline in inflation in recent months, said on Tuesday it would cut the official discount rate to 6.75 percent from 7.50 percent.
The cut will take effect on Wednesday, a Bank of Italy statement said. The last change to the discount rate was on October 23, when it was reduced by 75 basis points.
The Bank's fixed term advances, or Lombard rate, was simultaneously cut to 8.25 percent from a previous 9.00 percent.
A bank statement said that inflation had remained at moderate levels over the past few months, in line with objectives set for the current year.

Preliminary data from Italian cities released earlier on Tuesday showed that inflation, after falling to the lowest levels for years, was expected to remain steady at 2.6 percent year-on-year January, according to analysts.
The bank statement said it was closly watching trends in consumer demands, labour costs and price policies.
Monetary policy continues to remain targeted at seeking durable stability of the purchasing power of the lira, it added.
Central bank Governor Antonio Fazio said earlier this month that average consumer price inflation would fall below three percent in 1997 and hoped that the January 1997 figure would be a good one.
He said at the time that there were risks for inflation and these risks "come from public finance and labour costs and monetary policy has to reflect this".
He said it was also important to look at monthly variations in inflation and not just on the year on year data.
Analysts had expected the Bank of Italy to wait until after an agreement in a long-running dispute over a metalworkers contract before cutting official rates.
Treasury Minister Carlo Agzelio Ciampi expressed satisfaction over the rate cut in a statement, saying it would bring benefits to the entire economy, particularly for businesses.
"This way there are grounds for a stable and lasting economic recovery," Ciampi said.
